newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: FOCUS-IMF suspends $185 standby loan to Uzbekistan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-IMF suspends $185 standby loan to Uzbekistan.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) suspended a loan to Uzbekistan on Thursday amid growing criticism of foreign exchange controls in the resource-rich but secretive former Soviet republic.
The IMF said it had suspended disbursements of a $185 million standby loan to Uzbekistan because it had failed to meet the fund's inflation targets.

"Disbursements under the IMF stand-by arrangement have been postponed because of these developments," Mark O'Brien, the IMF's resident representative in Uzbekistan, told a news conference in the Uzbek capital Tashkent.
"Very tight financial policy...from the Central Bank must be combined with a full liberalisation of access to foreign exchange," he told reporters.
Journalists were preventing by Uzbek security officials from entering the IMF office inside the Uzbek central bank.
O'Brien, who held the news conference in the nearby offices of the United Nations, said an IMF mission planned to visit Tashkent to reassess the situation late in January.
O'Brien said Uzbekistan's target for 1996 annual inflation was set at around 25 percent but that the actual rate was likely to exceed 40 percent. He gave no exact figures.
"Uzbekistan's external trade account in 1996 was hit by lower international prices for cotton exports and a poorer than expected grain harvest," O'Brien said.
He said the Uzbek government had reacted by increasing credits to agriculture and limiting access to foreign exchange.

The resulting spread between Uzbekistan's official and black market rates has widened in recent weeks, with the official rate of 55 sums to the dollar way below the black market rate of 105-110 sums to the dollar on Thursday.
"Inflationary pressures increased and the exchange rates in the (interbank) auction, exchange bureaus and the kerb market diverged," said O'Brien.
In the last few weeks, many shops have had to shut in Tashkent due to a lack of foreign exchange.

Uzbek President Islam Karimov, the nation's former Communist Party boss who tolerates no dissent from the 23 million-strong population, has said he would prefer to see foreign exchange spent on importing new technologies rather than on "foreign chewing gum".
The suspension will come as a blow to Karimov who is ambitious to see the largely desert nation -- rich in gold, oil and gas -- become the "Singapore" of Central Asia.
The secretive Uzbek government rarely issues economic data, leaving observers heavily reliant on organisations like the IMF to find out what is going on in the republic's economy.
Last month, the World Bank representative in Tashkent, Hasso Molineus, was the first to bring official attention to the exchange controls.

"The increasing spread between the official and the black market rate of the sum reflects uncertainty in the investment community with regard to the impact of these controls," he told Reuters in an interview.
However, Molineus said the World Bank would continue its assistance programmes. Uzbekistan has already received $92 million of the IMF stand-by loan, agreed by the fund in December 1995.
